name: Alloderm lip augmentation

card.summary: Lip volume from processed donor skin (AlloDerm) placed in rolls in the lip; only a short description and one 2000 journal paper title exist.
card.note: No outcome data exist for this use.

quick.overview:
AlloDerm is donor skin from cadavers that has been processed to remove living cells. In lip augmentation, surgeons have placed it in small rolls in the lip or along the border of the lip to add size or sharpen the edge, according to Wikipedia.
A 2000 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery is titled "Alloderm lip augmentation", but no outcome data are available.
quick.mechanism: Rolled or layered donor dermal tissue is inserted into the lip mucosa to add bulk, or into the vermilion border to define it.
quick.risks: No specific complication data exist for this use. Wikipedia lists general lip augmentation complications such as swelling, bruising, asymmetry and lumpiness.

lead: AlloDerm lip augmentation uses processed donor (cadaver) dermis, with living cells removed, to add volume or definition to the lips. Wikipedia says it is placed in small rolls in the inner lip mucosa to increase lip size, or in the vermilion to sharpen the border of the lip.[1] People choose it for fuller or better-defined lips that last longer than a temporary filler, because the graft is tissue that integrates into the lip rather than a gel that is absorbed within months.[1][3]

A 2020 case report in Eplasty describes AlloDerm as a non-immunogenic acellular dermal allograft that is revascularized and integrated into surrounding tissue, with literature it cites reporting sustained volume at one-year follow-up, low resorption and high satisfaction after lip augmentation.[3] The same report traces the use of AlloDerm in facial soft-tissue augmentation to the 1990s.[3]

A 2000 letter titled 'Alloderm lip augmentation' by J. M. Gryskiewicz appeared in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery as a comment on an earlier article.[2] Wikipedia groups AlloDerm with other lip options including injectable fillers, fat grafting and implant strips, and lists risks common to lip augmentation such as swelling, bruising, asymmetry and implant extrusion.[1] No comparative trial of AlloDerm for lip augmentation was located.

chain: Donor dermis placed in rolls in the mucosa or along the lip border
Graft integrates and adds volume or a sharper outline
angle.text: The graft physically adds tissue to the lip, either as volume inside the lip or as a defined border at the vermilion. Surgeons and patients use it as an alternative to repeated filler sessions.[1][3]

infobox: AbbVie, per authors of a 2024 study[4]

paras: The material is human dermis processed to remove viable cells and used as a graft.[1] Wikipedia describes two placements in lip work: rolls inside the mucosa for volume and a strip at the vermilion to define the lip edge, and it does not give a duration for the result.[1]

Because the graft is acellular, the Eplasty authors describe it as non-immunogenic, producing no inflammatory response, and as able to be revascularized and integrated into surrounding tissue, creating bulk and a new plane of tissue.[3]

The 2020 Eplasty report states that the use of AlloDerm in soft-tissue augmentation was first described in the 1990s and cites a 1996 preliminary report on non-immunogenic acellular dermal allograft by Jones and colleagues, a 1998 paper on augmenting facial soft-tissue defects with AlloDerm by Achauer and colleagues, and a 1998 paper on lip augmentation using an AlloDerm graft by Tobin and Karas.[3] It also cites a 2002 study of one-year survival of AlloDerm and fat autograft in lip augmentation, and a report of early results of vermilion lip augmentation.[3]
A 2000 letter titled 'Alloderm lip augmentation' by J. M. Gryskiewicz was published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[2]

Wikipedia lists the other options: bovine collagen, which became the benchmark filler from about 1980 and is short-lasting; hyaluronic acid fillers, which usually last about six months to a year or more depending on the product; calcium hydroxylapatite gel, reported to last about two to five years; permanent PMMA microsphere fillers, which are generally not used in the lip body because they can show through the thin skin; expanded PTFE implant strips, which can shift or extrude; and fat grafting, often described as one of the best ways to maintain a semi-permanent fuller lip but with possible lumps or scarring and a second donor-site wound.[1]

Wikipedia notes that common reactions to lip augmentation include redness, swelling, itching and uneven lips, with swelling and bruising lasting from several days to about a week, that smoking slows healing, that overfilling produces the 'trout pout' look, and that outcomes depend heavily on the provider's skill.[1]
No studies found of AlloDerm for cosmetic lip augmentation reporting outcomes in this wiki's sources beyond a 2000 letter without an abstract and a 2020 single case report.[2][3]

The 2020 case report describes a 68-year-old professional trumpet player whose lower lip had a soft-tissue depression after Mohs surgery for squamous cell carcinoma, reconstructed with a mucosal advancement flap. Two hyaluronic acid filler attempts had failed because the filler extruded sideways. A 25 by 7 mm piece of thick AlloDerm was tunnelled into the area under a V-Y mucosal advancement flap; all incisions healed without issue over six months, he was cleared to play at eight weeks and regained trumpet playing except for high notes, and a 1 mL hyaluronic acid injection at four months improved high-pitch playing. The authors said this was the first report of acellular dermal matrix with a local advancement flap for a segmental lip defect, a functional rather than purely cosmetic use.[3]

A 2024 claims analysis in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open of 431 US adults who received AlloDerm in head and neck procedures found it used most with oral cavity reconstruction (35.3 percent), septal perforation repair or rhinoplasty (16.5 percent) and parotidectomy (13.0 percent); fewer than 1 percent (4 of 431) needed reoperation with AlloDerm in 30 days and 0.5 percent had graft complications. The authors were affiliated with the product's maker, and the study did not focus on lips.[4]

Specific risks of AlloDerm lip grafts are not described in the sources located beyond the 30-day reoperation and graft complication figures from the head and neck claims analysis.[4] Lip augmentation in general carries risks of bleeding, uneven lips, implant movement and extrusion, and some people are advised to avoid procedures with active cold sores, clotting or healing problems, or lidocaine allergy, according to Wikipedia.[1]

timeline.event: Preliminary report on non-immunogenic acellular dermal allograft for soft-tissue augmentation, as cited in the 2020 case report.[3]
Papers on AlloDerm for facial soft-tissue defects and for lip augmentation are published, as cited in the 2020 case report.[3]
'Alloderm lip augmentation' letter by Gryskiewicz is published in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery.[2]
Eplasty case report describes AlloDerm with a local advancement flap in lip reconstruction for a trumpet player.[3]
Claims analysis of AlloDerm use in head and neck procedures is published.[4]
